newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives plan local tax rebate for firms.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives plan local tax rebate for firms.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative party tried on Tuesday to take the initiative in the battle for the small business vote by proposing a local tax break for thousands of small firms.
Trade Secretary Ian Lang said that if the Conservatives were re-elected on May 1, they would reform the business rates (local corporate taxes) system by introducing a new rates allowance scheme.
This would mean that businesses would pay no rates at all on the first tranche of the rateable value of their premises.
Lang told a news conference in Birmingham he expected the allowance would be at least 1,000 pounds. The government would consult on the precise form and scale of the new scheme.
"Under this scheme, 93 percent of small businesses will benefit," he said.

"One hundred and forty thousand of the smallest properties will be taken out of rating altogether and 82 percent of small firms whose premises have a rateable value of 5,000 pounds or less will be big winners -- with reductions in their rates of between 15 percent and 100 percent."
He said the Conservative plan for rate relief for small businesses contrasted with the opposition Labour party's policy, which he said would give local councils control over business rates.

"After years of restraint under the Conservatives, Labour would let councils go on a spending spree at the expense of local business," Lang said. "What a disaster that would be. The truth is small business cannot trust Labour."
He was speaking at a news conference in Birmingham, the heartland of British small business, with Prime Minister John Major.
The focus on small firms was intended to pre-empt Labour's launch on Friday of a manifesto for small business.
